title: Organon
subtitle: The activities, designs, methods, techniques and instruments by which reality is observed and measured

families.name: Microscopy
families.principle: Scattering or absorption of light, electrons, or a scanned probe
families.observable: Spatial structure from millimetres to atomic scale
families.limit: Diffraction limit for light; electron optics and probe sharpness beyond it

families.name: Spectroscopy
families.principle: Absorption, emission or scattering of photons as a function of energy or wavelength
families.limit: Photon range and linewidth; surface sensitivity varies by technique

families.name: Separation
families.principle: Differential migration or partitioning of components

families.name: Diffraction
families.principle: Coherent scattering from a periodic structure

families.name: Sensing
families.principle: Transduction of a physical or chemical quantity into a signal
families.observable: Temperature, pressure, force, strain, chemical species

families.name: Remote Observation
families.principle: Collection of radiation from a distant source
families.observable: Position, spectrum and flux of a distant object
families.limit: Aperture and detector; the atmosphere for ground-based work

families.name: Electrical Measurement
families.principle: Deflection of a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, or the voltage drop across a known resistance
families.limit: Loading error (burden voltage) on one side, resolution and noise on the other

entries.name: Observation
entries.description: The registered attention to a system without necessarily intervening: the act that turns a state of the world into a record.

entries.name: Measurement
entries.description: The assignment of a value from a defined scale to a property, by a procedure that is stated and repeatable.

entries.name: Experiment
entries.description: An observation in which a condition is imposed by the observer, so that the effect of that condition can be separated from the rest.

entries.name: Sampling
entries.description: The selection of the part of the system that will be observed, and therefore the act that decides what the observation is evidence about.

entries.name: Monitoring
entries.description: Continuous or repeated observation against an objective, usually with an alarm or a threshold attached.

entries.name: Recording
entries.description: The preservation of an observation in a medium that can be re-examined after the event.

entries.name: Experimental Design
entries.description: The allocation of conditions to units, fixed before the data are seen, so that the comparison answers the question asked.

entries.name: Control Group
entries.description: The comparison arm that receives no treatment, so that the treatment effect is separated from time, selection and the measurement itself.

entries.name: Replication
entries.description: Independent repetition of the observation, within a study or across studies, which is what converts a single result into a claim about variability.

entries.name: Blinding
entries.description: Withholding the condition assignment from the observer or the subject, so that expectation cannot enter the measurement.

entries.name: Perturbation Method
entries.description: The routine that displaces the system from its state and reads the response: the general form of the controlled experiment.

entries.name: Stimulation Method
entries.description: The routine that drives a system with a defined input — electrical, optical, chemical — and measures the evoked output.

entries.name: Ablation Method
entries.description: The routine that removes a component and observes what the system can no longer do, the lesion logic of causal inference.

entries.name: Recording Method
entries.description: The routine that observes without imposing a condition, in order to capture the system's own behaviour.

entries.name: Imaging Method
entries.description: The routine that produces a spatially resolved representation of the system rather than a scalar measurement.

entries.name: Preparation Method
entries.description: The routine that makes the system observable — fixation, sectioning, labelling, cleaning, culturing — and therefore the routine that most determines what can be seen.

entries.name: Optogenetics
entries.description: The stimulation routine that makes a cell type responsive to light by expressing an opsin, so that one population can be driven while the others are silent.

entries.name: Combustion Analysis
entries.principle: Burn the sample and weigh or titrate the products
entries.limit: Milligram samples; the products must be separable
entries.description: Lavoisier's method, and the origin of quantitative chemistry: the sample is destroyed, and its composition is read from what it yields.

entries.name: Gravimetric Analysis
entries.principle: Precipitate the analyte and weigh it
entries.limit: Precipitation must be complete and the precipitate pure
entries.description: The reference method of nineteenth-century analytical chemistry: slow, exact, and still the calibration against which instrumental methods are checked.

entries.name: Titration
entries.principle: Add a reagent of known concentration until the equivalence point
entries.limit: The endpoint must be detectable; the reaction must be stoichiometric
entries.description: Descroizilles' method, and the workhorse of wet chemistry: a known reagent against an unknown sample, with the volume as the measurement.

entries.name: Elemental Analysis (CHNS)
entries.principle: Combust the sample and separate the gases chromatography
entries.observable: Mass fractions of C, H, N and S
entries.description: Liebig's and Dumas' refinement of combustion analysis into a routine instrument: the elemental composition of almost any organic sample in minutes.

entries.name: ICP-MS
entries.principle: Ionise in an inductively coupled plasma and separate by mass-to-charge
entries.description: The technique that made trace-element analysis routine: parts-per-trillion sensitivity across most of the periodic table.

entries.name: Mass Spectrometry
entries.principle: Ionise the molecule and measure mass-to-charge
entries.limit: Ionisation method decides which molecules are seen
entries.description: Thomson's parabola method, and the technique that turned molecular identity into a measurable quantity — extended by tandem methods into structure determination.

entries.name: X-ray Crystallography
entries.principle: Diffract X-rays from a crystal and invert the pattern
entries.limit: Requires a crystal; the phase problem must be solved
entries.description: Bragg's method, and the reason the atomic structure of matter is a measured rather than an inferred object — from minerals to proteins.

entries.name: Infrared Spectroscopy
entries.principle: Absorption of infrared photons by molecular vibrations
entries.limit: Water interference; overlapping bands in complex mixtures
entries.description: The vibrational fingerprint: which bonds are present, read from the frequencies they absorb.

entries.name: UV-Vis Spectroscopy
entries.principle: Absorption of ultraviolet and visible photons by electronic transitions
entries.description: The everyday quantitative spectroscopy: a colour is a concentration, and a band position is an electronic structure.

entries.name: NMR Spectroscopy
entries.principle: Resonance of nuclear spins in a magnetic field
entries.description: Bloch and Purcell's resonance, turned into the structural method of organic chemistry and, later, into imaging.

entries.name: ARPES
entries.principle: Photoelectric emission, with angle fixing k-parallel and photon energy tuning k-perpendicular
entries.limit: Occupied states only; few-angstrom surface depth
entries.description: The direct measurement of the band structure, which made the Fermi surface and the quasiparticle dispersion observable rather than inferred.

entries.name: Chromatography
entries.principle: Differential partitioning between a mobile and a stationary phase
entries.observable: Components of a mixture, separated in time
entries.description: Tsvet's separation of plant pigments, and the family that made mixture analysis routine.

entries.name: Gas Chromatography
entries.principle: Volatilise the sample and separate in a carrier gas
entries.limit: The sample must be volatile and thermally stable
entries.description: James and Martin's method, which brought separation to the petrochemical and environmental laboratory.

entries.name: HPLC
entries.principle: Pump a liquid mobile phase through a packed column under pressure
entries.limit: Pressure, column life and solvent consumption
entries.description: The high-resolution liquid separation that made pharmaceutical purity and biomolecule analysis practical.

entries.name: Thin-Layer Chromatography
entries.principle: Capillary migration along a coated plate
entries.description: The cheap, fast separation that survived every instrumental revolution because it answers in two minutes whether the reaction worked.

entries.name: Centrifugation
entries.principle: Separate by density under centrifugal force
entries.observable: Fractions by density or sedimentation rate
entries.description: Prandtl's method and the workhorse of biology: the cell is separated into its parts by how fast they sediment.

entries.name: Calorimetry
entries.principle: Measure the heat exchanged in a process
entries.limit: Heat loss; requires a controlled environment
entries.description: Lavoisier and Laplace's ice calorimeter, and the origin of thermochemistry: the heat of a reaction as a measured quantity.

entries.name: Spectrophotometry
entries.principle: Measure absorption at a fixed wavelength over time
entries.observable: Concentration as a function of time
entries.description: The kinetic version of UV-Vis: the reaction rate is read from the slope of an absorbance trace.

entries.name: pH / Redox Monitoring
entries.principle: Potentiometric response of an electrode
entries.limit: Drift and calibration; narrow linear range
entries.description: The electrode that made the state of a solution a continuous reading, and the ancestor of the modern process sensor.

entries.name: Cyclic Voltammetry
entries.principle: Sweep the potential and measure the current
entries.description: The electrochemical signature of a species, and the routine first look at any new redox system.

entries.name: Ion-Selective Electrode
entries.principle: A membrane potential that responds to one ion
entries.description: The sensor that made a single ion measurable in the field, from blood electrolytes to river water.

entries.name: Fluorescence / Luminescence
entries.principle: Excite and detect the emitted light
entries.observable: Presence and concentration of a fluorophore
entries.description: Stokes' observation, and the basis of every labelled assay: the detection of a molecule by the light only it emits.

entries.name: Radiochemical Tracer
entries.principle: Follow a radioisotope through a system
entries.observable: Pathway and rate of a labelled species
entries.description: Hevesy's method, and the invention of the tracer: a substance can be followed through a living system by its radioactivity.

entries.name: Passive Sampling
entries.principle: Accumulate the analyte in a sorbent over time
entries.description: The sampling method that measures exposure rather than a moment: what the environment did to the sampler over weeks.

entries.name: Soil / Water Sampling
entries.principle: Extract a representative portion of a natural matrix
entries.limit: Heterogeneity; the sample is not the field
entries.description: The routine that decides whether every later measurement is about the thing or about the spot.

entries.name: Immunoassay (ELISA)
entries.principle: Antibody binding, read by an enzymatic or fluorescent label
entries.description: Engvall and Perlmann's method, and the technique that gave biology a specific quantitative assay for almost any molecule.

entries.name: Enzymatic Assay
entries.principle: Measure the rate at which an enzyme converts its substrate
entries.description: The measurement of biological catalysis, and the reason enzyme kinetics is a quantitative science.

entries.name: DNA / RNA Sequencing
entries.principle: Read the order of nucleotides by synthesis or fragmentation
entries.limit: Read length against throughput; error rate
entries.description: Sanger and Maxam-Gilbert's method, and the technique that turned the genome into a readable document.

entries.name: Light Microscopy
entries.principle: Image with visible light through lenses
entries.observable: Structure down to the diffraction limit
entries.limit: About 200 nanometres; contrast must be created
entries.description: The instrument that founded biology as an observational science.

entries.name: Electron Microscopy
entries.principle: Image with electron optics
entries.description: Knoll and Ruska's instrument, which broke the diffraction limit of light by changing the wavelength.

entries.name: Fluorescence Microscopy
entries.principle: Excite fluorophores and image their emission
entries.description: The technique that bought specificity: seeing one molecule among thousands by making only it emit.

entries.name: Scanning Tunneling Microscopy
entries.principle: Tunnelling current from a sharp tip
entries.limit: Conducting surfaces; very small field of view
entries.description: Binnig and Rohrer's instrument, and the arrival of atomic-scale surface observation.

entries.name: Telescopic Observation
entries.principle: Collect radiation from a distant source with an aperture
entries.observable: Position, brightness and spectrum of the source
entries.description: Galileo's instrument, and the technique that made the sky an object of measurement rather than of description.

entries.name: Hemispherical Analyser
entries.description: The electrostatic energy filter that resolves photoelectron kinetic energy and emission angle — the component that makes ARPES a band-structure measurement.

entries.name: Chromatographic Column
entries.description: The stationary phase in a tube: the component whose chemistry decides what separates and how fast.

entries.name: Mass Analyser
entries.description: The magnetic, quadrupole or time-of-flight element that separates ions by mass-to-charge.

entries.name: Scanning Probe Tip
entries.description: The atomically sharp tip whose tunnelling current is the image; its sharpness is the resolution of the instrument.

entries.name: Spectrophotometer
entries.description: The monochromator and detector pair that turns absorbance at a wavelength into a number.

entries.name: Calorimeter
entries.description: The thermally isolated vessel in which the heat exchanged is measured.

entries.name: Synchrotron Light Source
entries.description: The tunable, bright photon source that lets ARPES probe different k-perpendicular values and reach the resolution the technique needs.

entries.name: Biosensor
entries.description: A transducer coupled to a biological recognition element, so that a molecule becomes a signal.

entries.name: Spin-Based Sensor
entries.description: A sensor that reads a magnetic field through spin-dependent transport or resonance, down to single-spin sensitivity.

entries.name: Glass pH Electrode
entries.description: The membrane electrode whose potential tracks hydrogen-ion activity; the sensor behind every pH reading.

entries.name: SI Unit
entries.description: The defined scale a measurement is expressed against; the definitions changed in 2019 from artefacts to constants.

entries.name: Calibration
entries.description: The comparison of an instrument against a reference of known value, and the operation that makes a reading traceable.

entries.name: Traceability
entries.description: The unbroken chain of comparisons that connects a working measurement to a national or international standard.

entries.name: Dataset
entries.description: The structured record of observations that later analysis treats as its input; its schema is part of the observation, not an afterthought.

entries.name: Spectrum
entries.description: A measured quantity resolved against energy, frequency or wavelength — the record a spectroscopy produces.

entries.name: Image
entries.description: A spatially resolved record of a signal, whose contrast mechanism is what it actually shows.

entries.name: Patent Dataset
entries.description: The corpus of patent filings treated as an observation record of invention, with the known biases of what is patented rather than invented.

entries.name: Measurement Theory
entries.description: The formal account of what a measurement is: a mapping from a property to a scale, with the conditions under which the mapping is meaningful.

entries.name: Measurement Uncertainty
entries.description: The quantified doubt attached to a value: the statement that makes a measurement a claim rather than a number.

entries.name: Validity and Reliability
entries.description: The two properties an observation must have — that it measures what it claims to, and that it does so consistently — and which reproducibility alone does not deliver.

entries.name: Quantum Measurement
entries.description: The measurement problem: the interaction between apparatus and system in quantum mechanics, where observation is not a passive read.

entries.name: Quantum Measurement Effects
entries.description: The observable consequences of measuring a quantum system — back-action, disturbance and the limits they set on simultaneous knowledge.

entries.name: Current Measurement
entries.principle: Pass the current through a known resistance or a magnetic field and read the deflection or the voltage
entries.limit: The meter must be inserted in the circuit, so it loads it; burden voltage and range switching set the accuracy
entries.description: Oersted's deflection of a compass needle by a current is the origin: the measuring instrument is a magnetic effect read as a number. The technique divides into direct insertion (ammeter, shunt) and non-invasive sensing (clamp meter, Hall sensor).

entries.name: Ammeter
entries.description: The instrument that measures current by being placed in series with the circuit: a moving-coil movement with a shunt across it, or a digital converter reading the drop across an internal resistor.

entries.name: Clamp Meter
entries.description: A current transformer or Hall sensor that measures the field around a conductor without breaking the circuit — the practical instrument for mains work.

entries.name: Shunt Resistor
entries.description: A low, known resistance in the current path whose voltage drop is the measurement; the element that both makes the reading possible and causes the burden voltage.
